items.bodyEn: Fukuroi is the twenty-seventh post town counted from Edo and also from Kyoto, so it calls itself the exact middle of the fifty-three. It was the last station added, in 1616, to break up the long stretch between Kakegawa and Mitsuke. Hiroshige drew it as an open-air tea stall, the kettle hung from a tree branch over the fire.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō No. 28 Fukuroi: Dechaya no zu; post-town records, 1616

items.bodyEn: Chabara mo ittoki: a bellyful of tea lasts for a while. Said when a stopgap tides you over, a cup at a roadside stall before the next town, a snack instead of lunch. The nuance is modest relief, not a real fix; the next meal still has to come.
items.ja: {茶腹|ちゃばら}も{一時|いっとき}

items.bodyEn: 景気 (keiki) is this station's word for the economy's mood, but it began as a term of poetry criticism: the scenery and atmosphere a waka evokes. In the Edo period it widened to 'the look of things', the liveliness of a market or town, and in modern Japanese settled on business conditions: keiki ga ii, times are good.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (日本国語大辞典), entry 景気 (けいき)

items.bodyEn: Both attach to a person, but they point different ways. Ni taishite (に対して) marks the target of an action or attitude: polite toward customers, strict toward students. Ni totte (にとって) marks the vantage point for a judgment: important for me, hard for beginners, seen from where they stand. If the sentence weighs value or difficulty, reach for ni totte.
items.ja: {私|わたし}にとって{大切|たいせつ}な{人|ひと}
items.kana: わたしにとってたいせつなひと
